problems.title: Publishing data
problems.statement: A producer writes value and then sets flag = 1; a consumer in another block spins on flag and then reads value.

parts.prompt: The producer needs, between the two writes…
The consumer's flag reads should be…

hints: Device-wide ordering; and the compiler must not cache the flag in a register.
problems.solution: (a) A device-wide fence orders the value before the flag. __syncthreads only covers the producer's block. (b) Volatile or atomic, or the compiler can hoist the load out of the loop and spin forever on a register.

problems.title: Scopes

parts.prompt: Which make shared-memory writes of one warp visible to another warp of the same block?
options: __threadfence_block() followed by a flag the other warp waits on
nothing: shared memory is always coherent instantly

problems.solution: __syncthreads (barrier plus visibility) or a block-scope fence with a flag. __syncwarp only covers its own warp. Shared memory is fast, not magically ordered.

problems.title: The grid barrier trap
problems.statement: A kernel launches 512 blocks; 8 blocks fit per SM on the GW-1's 16 SMs. Every block spins until a global counter reaches 512.

parts.prompt: Largest grid a cooperative launch would allow for this kernel?

hints: Resident blocks occupy the SMs while spinning.
problems.solution: 128 resident blocks spin forever waiting for 384 that need their SMs: deadlock. A cooperative launch refuses grids larger than what fits at once (128 here), which is what makes grid.sync() safe.

problems.title: Last block done
problems.statement: 256 blocks each write a partial, fence, and do old = atomicAdd(counter, 1).

parts.prompt: Value of old seen by the block that finishes last?

problems.solution: 255 = gridDim.x − 1. That block knows every other block has already published its partial (thanks to their fences before the atomic), so it can sum them.

problems.title: Message passing, litmus test
problems.statement: Thread A: data = 1; flag = 1; Thread B: r1 = flag; r2 = data; All start at 0; no fences, ordinary accesses; A and B are in different blocks.

parts.prompt: Can B end with r1 = 1 and r2 = 0?
With a fence between A's writes and an acquire (or fence) between B's reads?

hints: Relaxed models allow both store–store and load–load reordering as observed.
problems.solution: (a) Yes: the flag write can become visible first, or B's data read can be satisfied early. (b) Fence on both sides forbids it: this is the message-passing pattern done right.

problems.title: Store buffering
problems.statement: Thread A: x = 1; r1 = y; Thread B: y = 1; r2 = x; All start at 0.

parts.prompt: Without fences, is r1 = r2 = 0 possible?
With sequentially consistent fences between each thread's write and read?

hints: Each write may sit in a store buffer while the read goes ahead.
problems.solution: (a) Yes: both reads can run before either write is visible. (b) A full (seq_cst) fence forbids it. (c) Even x86, the strongest mainstream CPU model, allows this one; it's the classic reason Dekker-style locks need fences.

problems.title: Why dynamic tile ids
problems.statement: Decoupled look-back: tile i waits for tile i − 1's published prefix.

parts.prompt: Why take the tile id from an atomic counter instead of blockIdx.x?
options: It guarantees that tile i − 1 was claimed by a block that has already started, so waiting on it can't deadlock
blockIdx.x isn't available in every kernel

hints: Blocks aren't launched in index order.
problems.solution: If block 7 runs before block 6 is ever scheduled (and occupies the slot block 6 needs), waiting on blockIdx order can deadlock. Claiming ids in order of starting makes every awaited tile belong to a running or finished block.

problems.title: A spin loop that never ends
problems.statement: while (flag == 0) { } where flag is an ordinary global int written by another block.

options: load flag once into a register and spin on the register forever

hints: Nothing in the loop body tells the compiler that flag can change.
problems.solution: Hoisting the load is a legal optimisation for an ordinary variable: the loop becomes infinite. Use volatile, atomicAdd(&flag, 0) or cuda::atomic_ref with acquire loads.

problems.title: Launch boundaries as barriers
problems.statement: Scan $2^{20}$ ints. Each kernel launch costs 5 µs of overhead. Three-phase scan: 3 launches, 3n accesses. Single pass: 1 launch, 2n.
hints: Data time at 512 GB/s plus launch overhead.
problems.solution: (a) $15 + 24.6 = 39.6$ µs. (b) $5 + 16.4 = 21.4$ µs: 1.9× faster. For small problems launch overhead dominates, which also motivates CUDA Graphs and persistent kernels.

problems.title: Choosing a scope

parts.prompt: A flag between blocks of the same kernel on one GPU needs…
A flag between the GPU and a CPU thread, in pinned memory?

hints: The narrowest scope that includes everyone involved.
problems.solution: (a) Device scope. (b) System scope. Narrower scopes are cheaper; wider ones are required for correctness when more agents are involved.
